```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```
```{r}
#PART A
Respondent       <- 1:20
Sex              <- c(2,2,1,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,1,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,1,2)
FathersOccupation<- c(1,3,3,3,1,2,3,1,1,1,3,2,1,3,3,1,3,1,2,1)
PersonsAtHome    <- c(5,7,3,8,5,9,6,7,8,4,7,5,4,7,8,8,3,11,7,6)
SiblingsAtSchool <- c(6,4,4,1,2,1,5,3,1,2,3,2,5,5,2,1,2,5,3,2)
TypesOfHouses    <- c(1,2,3,1,1,3,3,1,2,3,2,3,2,2,3,3,3,3,3,2)

# Check lengths (all should be 20)
length(Respondent); length(Sex); length(FathersOccupation)
length(PersonsAtHome); length(SiblingsAtSchool); length(TypesOfHouses)

#Data frame
survey <- data.frame(Respondent, Sex, FathersOccupation,
                     PersonsAtHome, SiblingsAtSchool, TypesOfHouses)
print(survey)

# a. Describe
str(survey)
summary(survey)

# b. Dimensions
dim(survey)     # 20 6
nrow(survey)    # 20
ncol(survey)    # 6

#d. Means (done BEFORE factoring, since means of factors give NA)
survey_num <- survey
colMeans(survey_num)

#c. Factors
survey$Sex <- factor(survey$Sex, levels = c(1,2),
                     labels = c("Male","Female"))
survey$FathersOccupation <- factor(survey$FathersOccupation, levels = c(1,2,3),
                     labels = c("Farmer","Driver","Others"))
survey$TypesOfHouses <- factor(survey$TypesOfHouses, levels = c(1,2,3),
                     labels = c("Wood","Semi-Concrete","Concrete"))
str(survey)

# e. First five rows, all columns
survey[1:5, ]

# f. Types of houses
types_houses <- survey$TypesOfHouses
types_houses

#g. 
survey[survey$Sex == "Male" & survey$FathersOccupation == "Farmer", ]

#h. 
survey[survey$Sex == "Female" & survey$SiblingsAtSchool >= 5, ]

#Q5
sum(survey$Sex == "Male")   

##Q2: Each row is one respondent, so every column must have 20 values. A shorter vector would misalign answers, pairing one person's sex with another's house. data.frame() would also give an error.

##Q3: Sex, FathersOccupation and TypesOfHouses are nominal categories. PersonsAtHome and SiblingsAtSchool are real counts. Averaging Sex gives 1.85, which isn't a real sex, because the numbers are only labels.

##Q4: The output only shows "1", which someone without the legend could read as a score or rank instead of Male. Coded data hides its meaning until it is labeled, for example with factor().

##Q5: 3 of the 20 respondents are male. This sample is too small and too unbalanced (17 females) to generalize to a larger population, since one or two people could change the pattern.

##Q6: R stores these columns as plain numbers, so it treats them as numeric. It can't know they are categories unless you convert them with factor(). Storage (the type) and meaning are different things.

##Q7: The mean of PersonsAtHome (6.4) is meaningful: the average household has about 6 people. The mean of Sex (1.85) is not, because Sex is a category coded 1 and 2. For categories, report counts or proportions instead.
